newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Architect of Slovenian success wins second term.
newsitem.headline: Architect of Slovenian success wins second term.

text.p: Janez Drnovsek, who won a new term in office on Thursday, is credited with anchoring democracy and a thriving economy as prime minister in four of the five years since Slovenia seceded from Yugoslavia in 1991.
Drnovsek, 46, an economist and divorced father of one son, honed his political skills as the penultimate president of communist former Yugoslavia from 1989 to 1990.
The experience served him well as he needed to perform a delicate balancing act during his first term of office in Slovenia to keep a fragile left-right coalition from splitting apart.
He spurned pressure from his own centre-left Liberal Democrat Party last May to jettison the increasingly fractious Christian Democrats from the coalition.
Drnovsek said he intended to keep the government together in the national interest rather than pander to party politics.
His style drew praise from abroad and was a factor in consolidating a smooth transition from communist rule and a command economy, while other ex-Yugoslav republics turned to the gun.
Drnovsek's Liberal Democrats increased their share of the vote in a November 10 general election and remained the biggest party, winning 25 out of 90 parliamentary seats.
But an alliance of three right-wing parties just missed clinching an absolute parliamentary majority by just one seat, boosting their bid to form the new government.
Drnovsek won over smaller parties, including former communists, and the support of one Christian Democrat to clinch Thursday's parliamentary vote by a wafer-thin margin of 46 to 44.
Drnovsek has pledged to speed up privatisation, streamline the economy by cutting welfare payments and control inflation, which rose to 8.8 percent in 1996 from 8.6 percent a year ago.
But he may now depend on support from former communists and a leftist pensioners' party, which are sure to demand less stringent welfare cuts and try to give the transition a kinder social face.

Drnovsek crowned his first four years as leader by securing an association agreement with the European Union after patching up a row with Italy over the right of ethnic Italians to reclaim property they fled from at the end of World War Two.

The EU deal hinges on Slovenia bringing in laws to change the constitution to allow foreign nationals to buy real estate. That legislation would need a two-thirds majority in parliament and rightwing parties have vowed they will block the process.
Despite the difficulties ahead, Drnovsek predicts that Slovenia should become the first ex-Yugoslav republic to join the EU, possibly by the year 2001.

Slovenia's stability so near to the unpredictable Balkan region has made it a serious contender for NATO membership. Drnovsek has said entry into the EU and NATO would remain a priority in his next government.
